title: Is the slope zero?
objectives: Test a coefficient with a $t$ statistic.
Build a confidence interval for a slope and test against values other than zero

screens.title: Is the signal real?
screens.prose: Twelve months of a trading signal against the next month's return. The fitted slope is $\hat\beta = 0.30$: each point of signal adds 0.30% to the return. Its standard error is 0.20.
screens.question: How many standard errors is $\hat\beta$ from zero?

widget.label: Distance from zero in standard errors

hints.text: Distance in standard errors means dividing by the standard error.
The distance from zero is 0.30.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the slope's distance from zero by its standard error.

byKey.product: You multiplied the slope by its error. Divide instead: $0.30 / 0.20$.
byKey.gap: You subtracted the error from the slope. A distance in errors is a ratio: $0.30 / 0.20$.
byKey.flip: You divided the error by the slope. Put the slope on top: $0.30 / 0.20 = 1.5$.

explain.text: $0.30 / 0.20 = 1.5$. Suppose the true slope were zero. How often would noise alone push a fit 1.5 errors away? Answering that is a test of the slope.

screens.title: How rare is 1.5?
screens.prose: If the true slope is zero, the ratio $\hat\beta / \mathrm{SE}$ follows a $t$ distribution. The shaded tail is the chance of a ratio at least this large. Move both sliders and watch the tail.

derive.caption: Degrees of freedom {{nu}}. Shaded: ratios of {{fixed(t, 1)}} or more

screens.question: With ratio 1.5 and 10 degrees of freedom, what is the chance of a ratio at least 1.5 away from 0, in either direction?

widget.label: Chance of a ratio this far out

hints.text: Set the sliders back to 1.5 and 10.
The shaded tail covers only the right side.
The left tail below $-1.5$ is the same size. Double the shaded value.

feedback.correct: 0.165: about one data set in six.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the shaded tail at 1.5 and 10, then count both tails.

byKey.one-tail: That is the right tail only. A slope of $-0.30$ would be just as surprising, so double it.
byKey.inside: That is the chance of a ratio closer to 0 than 1.5. The question asks for the far side.
byKey.left: That is everything below 1.5. The test needs the tails beyond $\pm 1.5$.

explain.text: The tail beyond 1.5 holds 0.082, and the tail below $-1.5$ holds the same. Together that is 0.165, the **$p$-value**: about one data set in six shows a slope this far from zero by luck. Fewer degrees of freedom fatten the tails.

screens.title: Counting degrees of freedom
screens.prose: The ratio is the **$t$ statistic**, $t = \hat\beta / \mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta)$. Its degrees of freedom are those of $s$: the number of points minus the two numbers the line estimated.
screens.question: Our signal fit used 12 months. How many degrees of freedom does its $t$ statistic have?

hints.text: How many numbers did the line estimate?
The line estimated $\hat\alpha$ and $\hat\beta$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the number of estimated coefficients from the number of points.

byKey.n1: You used $n - 1$, as for a one-sample test. A line estimates two numbers, so subtract 2.
byKey.n: You used all 12 points. Two were spent fitting $\hat\alpha$ and $\hat\beta$.

explain.text: $s$ came from $\mathrm{SSE}/(n - 2)$, so the statistic carries $n - 2 = 10$ degrees of freedom. With 10 the tails are a little fatter than the normal's. With 1,000 they are almost the same.

screens.title: A range of plausible slopes
screens.prose: The 95% confidence interval is $\hat\beta \pm t_{0.975}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta)$. Here $t_{0.975}$ cuts off 2.5% in each tail. With 10 degrees of freedom $t_{0.975} = 2.228$.

state.caption: The middle 95% of $t_{10}$ runs from $-2.228$ to $2.228$

screens.question: What is the upper end of the 95% interval for the signal's slope?

hints.text: Multiply the cut-off by the standard error first.

byKey.normal: You used 1.96, the normal cut-off. With 10 degrees of freedom the cut-off is 2.228.
byKey.one-se: You added one standard error. A 95% interval reaches 2.228 errors out.
byKey.no-se: You added 2.228 itself. The cut-off is in standard errors, so multiply by 0.20 first.

explain.text: $0.30 \pm 2.228 \times 0.20$ gives $-0.146$ to $0.746$. The interval contains 0, which matches $p = 0.165 > 0.05$. At the same level the interval and the test always agree.

screens.title: Testing against 1
screens.prose: A stock's beta from 60 months is $\hat\beta = 1.30$ with standard error 0.25. The question is not whether beta is zero, but whether the stock moves more than the market: is $\beta = 1$?
screens.question: What is the $t$ statistic for testing $\beta = 1$?

hints.text: Measure the distance from the null value, not from 0.
The distance from 1 is 0.30.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract 1, then divide by 0.25.

byKey.vs-zero: You tested against 0: $1.30 / 0.25 = 5.2$. The question is about 1, so subtract 1 first.
byKey.no-se: 0.30 is the gap in beta units. Divide by the error, 0.25, to put it in standard errors.
byKey.flip: You subtracted the wrong way round. The estimate minus the null value is $+0.30$.

explain.text: $t = (1.30 - 1)/0.25 = 1.2$ on 58 degrees of freedom, so $p = 0.235$. The beta is far from 0 but not clearly above 1. Always test against the value that matters.

screens.title: Three points
screens.prose: A fit to just $n = 3$ points gives $\hat\beta = 2.0$ with standard error 0.5, so $t = 4.0$. That leaves $3 - 2 = 1$ degree of freedom.
screens.question: Is the slope significantly different from zero at 5%?

options.text: No: with 1 degree of freedom, $p = 0.156$
Yes: 4.0 is far beyond 1.96
options.why: You used the normal cut-off. With 1 degree of freedom the cut-off is 12.71.
That is the normal tail beyond 4. The $t_1$ tails are far fatter.

options.text: The test cannot be computed with 3 points
options.why: It can: $s$ exists with one degree of freedom. The test is just very weak.

hints.text: Which cut-off applies with 1 degree of freedom?
The caption gives the 5% cut-off for $t_1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare 4.0 with the $t_1$ cut-off, 12.71.

byKey.normal: You used 1.96, the normal cut-off. One degree of freedom makes $s$ very noisy, and the cut-off rises to 12.71.
byKey.normal-p: You read the normal tail. With one degree of freedom the two tails beyond 4 hold 0.156.

explain.text: One degree of freedom leaves $s$ almost unknown, so the $t$ tails are very fat. The 5% cut-off is 12.71, not 1.96. With three points only an enormous slope would count as evidence.

screens.title: Not significant
screens.prose: A signal's slope from 24 months is $\hat\beta = 0.40$ with standard error 0.30, so $t = 1.33$ and $p = 0.196$. The 95% interval runs from $-0.22$ to $1.02$. An analyst writes: the signal has no relationship with returns.
screens.question: What do the data actually say?

options.text: They cannot tell: slopes from $-0.22$ to $1.02$ all fit
The signal has no relationship with returns
options.why: You read not significant as zero. The interval holds 1.02, a strong effect, as well as 0.

options.text: There is a 19.6% chance the true slope is zero
options.why: You read $p$ as the chance the null is true. It is the chance of data this extreme if the slope were zero.

options.text: The signal adds exactly 0.40% per point
options.why: You took the estimate at face value. Its error is 0.30, almost as large as the slope.

hints.text: What range of slopes is consistent with the data?
Look at the interval, not just the $p$-value.
The interval contains 0, but it also contains slopes near 1.

feedback.correct: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which slopes the interval rules out.

byKey.none: You read not significant as no relationship. With 24 months the test has low power: a real slope of 0.40 is missed more often than not.
byKey.prob-null: You read $p$ as the chance the slope is zero. A $p$-value assumes the slope is zero and asks how surprising the data are.

explain.text: The test failed to reject zero, but the interval also holds slopes up to 1.02. With 24 months a true slope of 0.40 is detected only about a quarter of the time: the test has low power (testing, lesson 6). The honest summary is that we do not know yet.

screens.title: Why a $t$ with $n - 2$
screens.prose: Under the model $y_i = \alpha + \beta x_i + \epsilon_i$ with $\epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$ independent, build the statistic step by step.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $Z = \dfrac{\hat\beta - \beta}{\sigma / \sqrt{S_{xx}}} \sim N(0, 1)$: $\hat\beta$ is a weighted sum of normal $y_i$ with variance $\sigma^2 / S_{xx}$
$V = (n - 2)s^2 / \sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-2}$, independent of $Z$: the residuals have $n - 2$ free directions
$T = \dfrac{Z}{\sqrt{V / (n - 2)}} \sim t_{n-2}$: the definition of a $t$ variable

hints.text: A $t$ variable is a standard normal over the root of a scaled chi-squared.
Build the two ingredients first, in either order.
Standardise $\hat\beta$, then use $s^2$, then form the ratio, then cancel $\sigma$.

feedback.correct: $\sigma$ cancels, leaving a statistic we can compute.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Make the normal and the chi-squared pieces before you divide.

byKey.ratio: The ratio needs both $Z$ and $V$ defined first.
byKey.cancel: Cancelling $\sigma$ is the last step, once $T$ is a ratio.

explain.text: $Z$ uses the unknown $\sigma$, and $V$ uses it too. In the ratio $\sigma$ cancels, and what is left is $(\hat\beta - \beta)/\mathrm{SE}$. Its $n - 2$ degrees of freedom come from $s^2$.

screens.title: The test in one line
screens.prose: To test $\beta = \beta_0$: $$t = \frac{\hat\beta - \beta_0}{\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta)} \sim t_{n-2}, \qquad p = 2P(T_{n-2} > |t|).$$ The 95% interval is $\hat\beta \pm t_{0.975,\,n-2}\,\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta)$. Usually $\beta_0 = 0$; for a stock's beta it is often 1.
screens.question: The 95% interval excludes $\beta_0$ exactly when which holds?

options.why: You flipped the rule. A large $p$ means $\beta_0$ is inside the interval.

options.text: $|t| > 1.96$, whatever $n$ is
options.why: 1.96 is right only for large $n$. With few points the cut-off is larger.

options.text: $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta) < \hat\beta$
options.why: You compared the error with the estimate. The gap to $\beta_0$ must exceed $t_{0.975}$ errors.

hints.text: The interval is $\hat\beta$ plus or minus a number of errors.
$\beta_0$ is outside when the gap is more than $t_{0.975}$ errors.
Divide the gap by the error: that is $|t|$.

feedback.correct: The interval and the two-sided 5% test always agree.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write when $|\hat\beta - \beta_0|$ exceeds $t_{0.975}\,\mathrm{SE}$.

explain.text: $\beta_0$ lies outside $\hat\beta \pm t_{0.975}\mathrm{SE}$ when $|\hat\beta - \beta_0| > t_{0.975}\mathrm{SE}$. Dividing by the error gives $|t| > t_{0.975}$. That is the same as $p < 0.05$.

screens.title: Is the alpha real?
screens.prose: A strategy's 36-month record, regressed on the market, gives a monthly alpha of 0.45% with standard error 0.30%. Write a test you can reuse. `stats.t.sf(x, df)` is $P(T > x)$.
screens.question: Complete `t_test` so it returns $t$ and the two-sided $p$-value with $n - 2$ degrees of freedom.

widget.starter:
from scipy import stats

def t_test(est, se, n, null=0.0):
    t = ...
    p = ...   # two-sided, n - 2 degrees of freedom
    return t, p
widget.solution:
from scipy import stats

def t_test(est, se, n, null=0.0):
    t = (est - null) / se
    p = 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t), n - 2)
    return t, p
widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. Each returns [t, p] rounded to 6 places and compared with math.isclose. The first run loads SciPy, which takes 10 to 20 seconds.

hints.text: $t$ is the distance from `null` in standard errors.
`stats.t.sf(abs(t), n - 2)` is one tail beyond $|t|$.
Double the one tail for a two-sided $p$-value.

feedback.correct: For the strategy, $t = 1.5$ and $p = 0.143$: not evidence of skill yet.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the sign handling with `abs(t)` and the degrees of freedom, $n - 2$.

explain.text: The alpha is 1.5 errors from zero, and $p = 0.143$. One strategy in seven with no skill would look this good over 36 months. The same function tests a beta against 1 with `null=1.0`.

ideas: $t = (\hat\beta - \beta_0)/\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta)$ measures the gap to the null value in standard errors, with $n - 2$ degrees of freedom.
The two-sided $p$-value counts both tails. The 95% interval $\hat\beta \pm t_{0.975}\mathrm{SE}$ excludes $\beta_0$ exactly when $p < 0.05$.
Significant does not mean causal, and not significant does not mean zero: read the interval.

formula.name: t test for a slope
formula.note: With very few points the cut-off is huge: 12.71 for $n = 3$.

summary.trap: Not significant is not no relationship. With little data the test has low power, so the interval is wide.

quiz.prose: Across 500 stocks, next year's return is regressed on the number of analysts covering each stock. The slope has $t = 4.1$.
quiz.question: What can we conclude?

options.text: Coverage and returns are related; this alone does not show coverage causes returns
Adding an analyst raises a stock's return
options.why: You read significance as cause. Large, liquid firms attract analysts and differ in many other ways.

options.text: Each analyst adds 4.1% to the return
options.why: You read the $t$ statistic as the slope. $t$ measures evidence, not size.

options.text: The effect is real with probability 0.9999
options.why: You read $1 - p$ as the chance the effect is real. A $p$-value is not that.

feedback.correct: Significant means unlikely to be luck, not causal.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate evidence of a link from evidence of cause.

explain.text: $t = 4.1$ says the slope is very unlikely to be zero. It says nothing about why. A third factor, such as firm size, can drive both coverage and returns.

quiz.prose: A fit to $n = 22$ points gives $\hat\beta = 0.80$ with standard error 0.25. With 20 degrees of freedom $t_{0.975} = 2.086$.
quiz.question: What is the lower end of the 95% confidence interval?

byKey.normal: You used 1.96. With 20 degrees of freedom the cut-off is 2.086.
byKey.one-se: You went one error down. A 95% interval reaches 2.086 errors.

explain.text: $2.086 \times 0.25 = 0.522$, so the interval runs from 0.279 to 1.322. It excludes 0, so the slope is significant at 5%.

quiz.prose: A utility stock's beta from 60 months is $\hat\beta = 0.85$ with standard error 0.05.
quiz.question: Test $\beta = 1$. What do you conclude at 5%?

options.text: $t = -3.0$, $p = 0.004$: beta is below 1
$t = 17$: beta is above 1
0.85 is close to 1, so beta is 1
options.why: You judged the gap by eye. The error is only 0.05, so a gap of 0.15 is three errors.

options.text: $t = 3.0$: beta is above 1
options.why: You subtracted the wrong way round. $0.85 - 1 = -0.15$.

feedback.correct: Three errors below 1: a defensive stock.

explain.text: $t = (0.85 - 1)/0.05 = -3.0$ on 58 degrees of freedom, and $p = 0.004$. The stock moves clearly less than the market.

quiz.prose: A slope has $t = 2.5$ on 30 degrees of freedom. $P(T_{30} > 2.5) = 0.0091$.
quiz.question: What is the two-sided $p$-value?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count both tails.

byKey.one: That is one tail. A slope as far below zero counts too, so double it.
byKey.complement: That is the chance of a smaller statistic. The $p$-value is the far tails.

explain.text: Each tail beyond $\pm 2.5$ holds 0.0091, so $p = 0.018$. The slope is significant at 5% but not at 1%.
